Summary
A sound election system has to do two things simultaneously: Prevent voter fraud while ensuring that every eligible vote is counted. Proposition 39 is arguably an attempt to improve electoral confidence while minimizing negative effects on ballot access.
Proposition 39 requires that voters provide either state-issued identification to vote in person or the last four digits of a government-issued identification number to vote by mail-in ballot, similar to many other states. It also requires that elections officials publish regular eligibility audits of voter rolls. Lastly, it mandates that California create an alternate state ID card so that those who don’t have other forms of ID, like a driver’s license, are able to vote.
Given that over 80 percent of California voters make use of mail-in ballots, Proposition 39’s greatest impacts will be on mail-in voting rather than in-person voting. California’s recent shift to all-mail elections has vastly expanded the ease of voting and, as a result, voter participation. It also has opened up a new, more rewarding avenue for voter fraud. There is no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California. Yet instances of fraud have been uncovered, and the increase of mail-in voting has coincided with decreasing confidence in the honesty of elections.
Because California’s existing election systems already requires elections officials to contact voters—by mail, email, and phone—to “cure” their mail-in ballot of any deficiencies and allows voters twenty-two days after Election Day to do so, expanding identification requirements does not seem likely to substantially inhibit valid votes from being counted.
Realistically, there is an inherent trade-off between election legitimacy and making voting easy. This measure effectively asks voters whether increased legitimacy is worth making voting slightly more difficult.

Summary
A sound election system has to do two things simultaneously: Prevent voter fraud while ensuring that every eligible vote is counted. Proposition 39 is arguably an attempt to improve electoral confidence while minimizing negative effects on ballot access.
Proposition 39 requires that voters provide either state-issued identification to vote in person or the last four digits of a government-issued identification number to vote by mail-in ballot, similar to many other states. It also requires that elections officials publish regular eligibility audits of voter rolls. Lastly, it mandates that California create an alternate state ID card so that those who don’t have other forms of ID, like a driver’s license, are able to vote.
Given that over 80 percent of California voters make use of mail-in ballots, Proposition 39’s greatest impacts will be on mail-in voting rather than in-person voting. California’s recent shift to all-mail elections has vastly expanded the ease of voting and, as a result, voter participation. It also has opened up a new, more rewarding avenue for voter fraud. There is no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California. Yet instances of fraud have been uncovered, and the increase of mail-in voting has coincided with decreasing confidence in the honesty of elections.
Because California’s existing election systems already requires elections officials to contact voters—by mail, email, and phone—to “cure” their mail-in ballot of any deficiencies and allows voters twenty-two days after Election Day to do so, expanding identification requirements does not seem likely to substantially inhibit valid votes from being counted.
Realistically, there is an inherent trade-off between election legitimacy and making voting easy. This measure effectively asks voters whether increased legitimacy is worth making voting slightly more difficult.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The original title was “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” but this was changed by the California attorney general to “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification.” Ballot measure proponents challenged the new name as misleading, but the deputy attorney general argued that the title is only misleading if read in isolation. The Sacramento Superior Court ruled the changed title and summary were “sufficient.”
Measure’s own name: The California Voter ID Initiative (AG No. 25-0007A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: Voters must show government-issued ID to vote in person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number on their mail-in ballot envelopes. The state must offer a free voter ID card and conduct regular audits of voter rolls to verify eligibility and citizenship.
A vote NO means: California keeps its current system, which asks for no ID at the polls and verifies mail ballots by signature match.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0007A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0007 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-007)
1. What would it do?
More than two-thirds of states require a voter to provide identification to receive a ballot, and recent national polls by the Pew Research Center, Rasmussen Reports, and Gallup show that over 75 percent of US adults support photo ID requirements to vote. California is one of the remaining states that does not ask for any identification for in-person voting. Under this measure, anyone voting in person would have to present a government-issued ID to receive a ballot.
A similar requirement would apply to mail-in ballots. Under the measure, a mail-in voter would have to write the last four digits of a unique government-issued identification number (such as Social Security number, driver’s license number, or Voter ID card) on the ballot envelope. That number would be matched against the voter’s registration record before the ballot is counted.
For context, Minnesota already uses a similar system that requires a voter-specific identification number to verify mail-in ballots. To further ensure election integrity, Minnesota law also requires that absentee voters show their blank ballot to a witness (who must be a US citizen, notary, or public official) prior to the voter filling it out, and then requires that witness’s signature on the signature envelope certifying that the ballot was completed privately. Before the ballot is recorded at least two members of the absentee ballot board (either election officials or representatives of different political parties) review each signature envelope to ensure that it matches the voter’s name, address, signature, and voter identification number and has a witness signature.
Proposition 39 includes three more parts to facilitate voter identification and the validation of voter rolls. First, it requires the state to provide a free voter ID card on request, reducing the ballot access issues that can be caused by using a driver’s license as the default identification. Second, it requires the California Secretary of State’s office and county election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, use government data to verify citizenship attestations, and publicly report each year what share of the rolls has been citizenship-verified. Lastly, it is self-executing, such that every two years the California State Auditor’s Office must publish an audit of state and county election officials’ compliance. It also empowers any citizen to seek judicial review and remedy if they believe that state or county officials are not complying with the constitutional amendment.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0007A1, “California Voter ID Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf) (as amended August 7, 2025)
Key language: “Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration.”
What it amends:
Adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution, the article that governs voting. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot simply repeal it, and it directs the legislature to enact implementing laws and to provide for military and overseas voters consistent with federal law.
3. Who, What, Where, When, Why?
What would it change about voting?
It would require a government-issued ID for in-person voting or the provision of the last four digits of a government ID number for mail voting. It requires the state to provide a free state ID card on request. Lastly, it mandates that the state regularly verify the citizenship of registered voters and report the results of that audit.
Where would it take effect?
Statewide, in every election.
When would it take effect?
The measure is self-executing on passage, such that the legislature is directed to enact implementing laws, and the state auditor is directed to publish an audit of compliance by state and county election officials in every odd-numbered year.
Why add identification rules to the voting process?
The proponents’ stated goals for this measure are to promote public confidence in the electoral process and voting results by deterring and detecting fraud, confirming voter eligibility, and minimizing voter impersonation.
4. Trade-offs
The 2020 presidential election results were controversially challenged as being manipulated by widespread voter fraud—an allegation that was believed by three out of every eight voters. The extensive mail-in voting allowed due to COVID-19 pandemic concerns was blamed as part of this alleged fraud. However, documented cases of election fraud are rare, and the most rigorous review of the 2020 election did not find evidence to support claims of systematic fraud.
A more general issue is that voter fraud statistics only measure the fraud that we have been able to detect and, more importantly, the fraud that was perpetrated within the system as it previously existed. The next sections examine:
The ways that elections have substantially changed over the last fifty years, with major changes accelerating over the last decade
How these changes provide a rational argument for those concerned with voter fraud
How the changes, at least in part, seem to be linked to declining voter confidence in elections
The type of fraud inhibited by ID requirements for in-person voting—where one person impersonates another at the polling place—is the rarest documented form of voter fraud. This doesn’t make in-person voter identification unimportant, but in-person voter fraud is arguably the smallest part of the problem. The elephant in the room, so to speak, is the significant increase in mail-in voting.
In brief summary, California’s mail-in voting system verifies eligibility mainly through the voter’s own attestation that they are who they say they are and by matching their signature to a previous signature on record (see the California Decides FAQ: How Elections Are Run (https://www.hoover.org/research/how-elections-are-run) for additional information). The lack of a rigorous means to validate who specifically filled out the mail-in ballot—which is done in private, far away from the public view of voting centers—increases the potential for voter fraud. Furthermore, the lack of clearer voter identification mechanisms means that investigations into whether voter fraud occurred will struggle to definitively certify the lack of fraud. That validation gap is precisely the proponents’ argument for building a more complete verification infrastructure.
Changes to US Elections
US elections have seen major changes since states started expanding absentee mail-in voting in the 1970s. This, like early in-person voting, has led to large decreases in voting at public polling locations on Election Day. In the last two presidential elections, over 80 percent of Californians voted by mail.
At the national level:
In-person voting on Election Day has been steadily decreasing, from around 90 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 60 percent in 2016. That percentage dropped to 31 percent in 2020 and recovered slightly to 40 percent in 2024.
Meanwhile, absentee/mail-in voting has been steadily increasing, from around 8 percent of votes cast in the mid-1990s to 21 percent of votes cast in 2016. During the pandemic mail-in ballots surged to 43 percent of votes cast in 2020 and then returned to the previous trend, accounting for 29 percent of votes in 2024.
Early in-person voting has seen a similar upward trajectory, from 2–3 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 19 percent in 2016. The trend has accelerated faster than mail-in voting, with early in-person voting accounting for 26 percent of votes cast in 2020 and 31 percent of votes cast in 2024.
The shift away from in-person voting on Election Day seems to have increased voter anxiety about the electoral process, perhaps due to the reduced ability to identify fraud and therefore a perception that fraud would be easier to employ. Currently, eight states now practice all-mail elections (where every eligible voter receives a ballot by mail), twenty-nine more allow no-excuse absentee voting, and forty-seven allow some form of early in-person voting.
California was the first state to allow no-excuse absentee voting, starting in 1979. By 2012, a majority of California ballots were submitted by mail. Starting in 2018, the state allowed county elections officials to shift to an all-mail election, and the state itself adopted an all-mail ballot starting in 2020. This led to over 86 percent of ballots being cast by mail in 2020, followed by over 80 percent in 2024.
Concerns about Ballot Harvesting
In California, concerns about voter fraud have probably been exacerbated by legislation passed in 2016 that legalized unlimited third-party ballot collection, a practice that is more generally known as ballot harvesting. It allows any person to collect and submit any number of mail-in ballots, including paid campaign workers and volunteer advocates. The same year, other legislation enabled county election officials to mail every registered voter a ballot, expand early in-person voting, and create ballot drop box locations with 24/7 access.
In theory, the mail-in ballots should already be filled out and sealed when given to the ballot harvester, such that there’s little opportunity for the harvester to view or change the vote. There is no way to ensure this, but it’s also relevant to highlight that changing another person’s ballot (or filling it out without their approval) has never been legal and is the most fundamental form of voter fraud.
Opponents of ballot harvesting argue that the practice breaks the intrinsic chain of custody for mail-in ballots—from the voter to US Postal Service staff to elections officials—and therefore impugns the integrity of such ballots. Proponents argue that it enables greater voter participation. Both things can be simultaneously true: Many voters likely find it easier to vote, and unscrupulous political agents also have greater ability to practice fraud (regardless of whether they have actually exercised that ability to date or have done so in statistically measurable ways).
By law, the ballot harvester is required to provide their name and signature on the ballot return envelope. However, there currently doesn’t seem to be any way to validate that ballot harvesters are adhering to this requirement, because there’s nothing that distinguishes a ballot submitted by a ballot harvester from one submitted by the voter. The current system effectively places ballot harvesters on the honor system to provide that information on each ballot they submit via mail or ballot drop box, because without providing that information it appears to the elections officials that the voter submitted the ballot themselves.
Decreasing Voter Confidence and Perceived Election Honesty
At the national level, voters’ confidence in whether their own vote is counted correctly is generally high, but there is reduced confidence in whether national voting in general is counted correctly. There is also clearly declining confidence in the general honesty of elections.
It’s important to note that while voter confidence has indeed decreased over recent decades, in the short run a major part of this sentiment seems to be driven by whether a voter’s preferred candidate won the election (called the winner-loser effect). This can be particularly seen in the 2024 election, when Republican-leaning voters went into the election with very low confidence in whether their vote would be counted and then reported greater confidence in US elections following President Trump’s victory. Democratic-leaning voters shifted in the opposite direction, but the size of the change was not as substantial.
5. Conclusion
Passage of Proposition 39 would bring California into line with most other states. Voter ID requirements receive broad, bipartisan support—more than 75 percent of voters support requiring a photo ID to vote—and the ballot measure addresses a real gap in how the state verifies voter eligibility.
The trade-off for greater electoral confidence is that voter ID requirements can cause some eligible ballots to be rejected for honest mistakes. However, the legislature can effectively solve this problem by employing a system similar to that which California already uses, which requires election officials to contact voters to rectify problems with the identification the voter submitted and provides twenty-two days after Election Day to do so.
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.
(d) The loss of billions in federal funding further
stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to
reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source
of health coverage for half of all births statewide.
Recent years have seen closures of vital maternity
wards and emergency departments, all attributed in
large part to low Medi-Cal reimbursement rates.
(g) Investment in Medi-Cal is an investment in every
family’s health security. It keeps primary care clinics
and community health centers open across towns and
cities, allowing people to manage chronic conditions,
prevent costly complications, and live longer, healthier
lives. Every dollar cut from these programs

Now I have a very good picture. Let me summarize the evidence:

**What Prop 39 does:**
1. Requires government-issued ID for in-person voting
2. Requires last 4 digits of a government ID number on mail ballot envelopes (must match the one designated in voter registration)
3. Requires election officials to make "best efforts" to verify citizenship of registered voters using government data
4. Creates a free state voter ID card
5. Requires annual reporting of citizenship verification percentage, biennial State Auditor compliance audits
6. Requires legislative action for full implementation
7. Costs: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year

State shall provide, at no charge, a voter ID card for use

# My answer: **No**

Here's how I got there, based on extensive research into the measure itself, the Legislative Analyst's analysis, the academic literature, and real-world evidence from states that have tried this.

## What Prop 39 actually does

It's a constitutional amendment that would require government ID for in-person voting, and — critically — would require the last four digits of a government ID number (matching the one on your registration) on every mail ballot envelope, or the ballot doesn't get counted. It also adds citizenship-verification "best efforts," a free state voter ID card, and audits.

## Why the evidence points to No

**1. The fraud it targets is vanishingly rare.** In-person voter impersonation — the thing voter ID prevents — is the rarest documented form of fraud. Even the Heritage Foundation's own database (the strongest pro-ID source) documents only about 0.02–0.08 cases per 100,000 people per year, and most rigorous studies find no detectable effect of ID laws on fraud. Even the Hoover Institution's sympathetic analysis concedes there's "no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California."

**2. The mail-ballot provision has a documented track record of failure — in a state that votes overwhelmingly by mail.** ~85% of California ballots are cast by mail, so this provision is the measure's real core. Texas passed a nearly identical rule (ID number must match your registration record on the envelope). The result in the first election: mail ballot rejections jumped from ~1% to **12.4%**, roughly 30,000 voters had applications or ballots rejected, ~90% never ended up participating, and Black, Latino, and Asian voters were rejected at significantly higher rates than white voters. That's orders of magnitude more eligible voters disenfranchised than fraudulent votes prevented.

**3. The core rationale — "increasing trust in elections" — is empirically unsupported.** This is the striking part: multiple peer-reviewed studies (Cantoni & Pons, Ansolabehere & Persily, Stewart et al., Bowler et al.) consistently find that voter ID laws do **not** increase voter confidence or reduce perceived fraud. If anything, the polarized fight over them seems to reduce trust. So the main claimed benefit doesn't materialize, while the rejection costs do.

**4. Real costs and implementation risk.** The Legislative Analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year — and notes savings would partly come from *fewer registered voters, including eligible voters lacking ID*. Notably, the amendment itself contains **no cure process** for mismatched or missing ID digits (unlike California's current 22-day signature cure window); it leaves those details to implementing legislation in a Legislature whose leadership opposes the measure — a recipe for a botched rollout.

## The strongest Yes arguments (which I took seriously)

- Standard polling-place ID laws have shown little to no measurable turnout decline in the best recent research (Cantoni & Pons), so the "suppression" charge is weaker than opponents claim.
- Voter ID polls at 75%+ nationally including majorities of Democrats; most states require some ID.
- The free voter ID card addresses access concerns, and ID numbers are arguably more reliable than signature matching (though California's signature system rejects only ~0.9% of mail ballots, with a cure process — vs. Texas's 12% under ID matching).

## Bottom line

The trade the measure offers is: spend tens-to-hundreds of millions annually and risk Texas-style ballot rejection rates for 13+ million mail voters, in exchange for deterring a nearly nonexistent form of fraud and a trust boost that research shows doesn't actually materialize. The costs are demonstrated and large; the benefits are hypothetical and empirically unproven. **Vote No.**

39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
CON
No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. Don’t believe the lies. Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.
PROP. 39 IS FUNDED BY MAGA RIGHTWING BILLIONAIRES. Follow the money. MAGA billionaires have spent millions spreading election lies. Republican operatives have pushed this voter suppression agenda for years. They want Trump to have unlimited power so they get more tax breaks for the rich while cutting funding to healthcare and schools for the rest of us.
California election officials already verify voters. Prop. 39 just ADDS EXTRA HURDLES for citizens. THE FACTS DON’T LIE. When Texas tried this, they threw out 12 times more mail ballots than California.
Prop. 39 creates new threats of identity theft. No citizen should have to choose between their privacy and their right to vote.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found that Prop. 39 could COST HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS EACH YEAR—read it for yourself. MAGA extremists want to use your taxpayer dollars to buy Trump an expensive gift: blocking eligible voters and giving the Big Lie a win in California. We won’t fall for it.
PROP. 39 TRIES TO DISTRACT US from how Trump and his billionaire friends have failed Americans. Hospitals are closing. Fire victims are still waiting for help. Groceries and housing costs are more expensive than ever. Now they want to use Prop. 39 to control our elections and avoid accountability.
NO KINGS. NO LIES. NO PROP. 39.
Alex Padilla , U.S. Senator for California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39
VOTE NO. Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.
STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. Now he wants to undo our freedoms and democracy with Prop. 39. Trump’s cronies want to rig California elections so they can seize and keep control of Congress and the White House. Trump will do whatever it takes to tear apart our right to vote, dodge accountability, and hold onto authoritarian power.
CALIFORNIANS WON’T FALL FOR IT. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop. 39. Don’t let California become the next state where politicians pick which voters count.
WASTES HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS.
Trump and his accomplices want California to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to chase their election lies and conspiracy theories. Californians are struggling, and Trump wants YOU to pay for his conspiracies.
PUTS YOUR IDENTITY AT RISK. Prop. 39 will make every vote by mail voter include their personal details on their return envelope—making voters easy targets for identity theft. Voters would have to choose between voting and protecting their privacy.
BLOCKS CITIZENS FROM VOTING. Prop. 39 adds new hurdles—voters would have to include a personal ID number on their ballot envelope that has to exactly match state records. Get one digit wrong, and a valid ballot could get thrown out. If you don’t take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all. And if the address on your ID is not up to date or your name is misspelled—your vote might be rejected.
PUSHES OUT VOTERS. “Free” state IDs aren’t free: voters still pay for transportation, time off work, and costs like childcare or getting required documents. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and the millions of women who changed their names at marriage are hit hardest. These unfair barriers help politicians choose their voters instead of the other way around.
TRUMP LIES TO GRAB POWER. DON’T LET THOSE LIES TAKE AWAY YOUR VOTE.
PROTECT YOUR VOICE. PROTECT YOUR VOTE. VOTE NO.
Learn more at CAforVotingRights.org
David Trujillo , Executive Director
ACLU California Action
Darius Kemp , California State Director
Common Cause
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 39
PROP. 39 IS BIPARTISAN—NOT ABOUT DONALD TRUMP OR GAVIN NEWSOM
Prop. 39 gives California a bipartisan solution for election security. While politicians in D.C. fight over partisan control of elections, Californians can adopt our own solution: Voter ID. Opponents will claim this measure is about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom. It isn’t. Prop. 39 is a California solution to growing mistrust in our elections. Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisans encourage you to reject the big-money partisan allegations and vote yes on Prop. 39 to encourage voter participation and protect our elections.
PROP. 39 IMPROVES ELECTION MANAGEMENT
Prop. 39 improves the accuracy of our voter lists and requires independent audits to strengthen election management.
VOTER ID INCREASES TRUST IN ELECTIONS
States with voter ID laws have not seen decreases in voter participation. When voters trust elections, participation increases.
YES ON PROP. 39
Opponents will claim this is about national politics or that Voter ID suppresses voters. Don’t be fooled. Prop. 39 is supported by Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisans, as well as men, women, young, and old—Californians across many communities.
If you believe California should strengthen trust in elections while keeping voting accessible for eligible voters, vote YES on Prop. 39 for a clean, bipartisan California solution.
Johnathan Hale , Executive Director
The Transparency Foundation
Cynthia Kaui , Executive Director
California Women’s Leadership Association
Ed Cervantes , President
Latino American Political Association

# Obstacles to Estimating Voter ID Laws’ Effect on TurnoutJustin Grimmer
## Abstract
Widespread concern that voter identification laws suppress turnout among racial and ethnic minorities has made empirical evaluations of these laws crucial.
But problems with administrative records and survey data impede such evaluations.
We replicate and extend Hajnal, Lajevardi, and Nielson’s 2017 article, which concludes that voter ID laws decrease turnout among minorities, using validated turnout data from five national surveys conducted between 2006 and 2014.
We show that the results of their article are a product of data inaccuracies, the presented evidence does not support the stated conclusion, and alternative model specifications produce highly variable results.
When errors are corrected, one can recover positive, negative, or null estimates of the effect of voter ID laws on turnout, precluding firm conclusions.
We highlight more general problems with available data for research on election administration, and we identify more appropriate data sources for research on state voting laws’ effects.

The academic literature on voter ID laws and turnout is actually quite mixed — the best recent research (Cantoni & Pons, Grimmer & Yoder) finds minimal effects on turnout, while GAO found decreases in Kansas and Tennessee. Interesting.

But Prop 39 is not just a standard voter ID law — it has a mail ballot provision requiring the last four digits of a government-issued ID number on the ballot envelope, which is similar to Texas SB 1. The Texas experience saw mail ballot rejection rates shoot up dramatically (from ~1-2% to ~12% in the 2022 primary). That's a key difference: Prop 39 applies ID requirements to mail voting, which most Californians use (13 of 16 million votes are by mail).

Let me research:
1. The Texas experience with mail ballot ID requirements (SB 1) — rejection rates.
2. The claim that similar requirements "throw out 12 times more mail ballots."
3. The SAVE Act and noncitizen voting fraud evidence — how prevalent?
4. Also the claim about funding — MAGA billionaires. Let me check the campaign contributions.
5. The Hoover Institution piece by Justin Grimmer arguing the effects are minimal.

Also, I should consider the tradeoffs: The measure also requires citizenship verification of voter rolls, free voter ID, audits. The cost is tens of millions to low hundreds of millions per year.

Key considerations for my recommendation:
- Voter fraud (especially in-person impersonation, which is what voter ID addresses) is extremely rare. The existing system uses signature verification for mail ballots, and ID checks for first-time voters who registered without providing ID.
- The specific mail-ballot provision (last 4 digits of ID on envelope) caused massive ballot rejection rates in Texas when first implemented.
- Research on standard voter ID effects on turnout: mixed but generally small effects.
- California is overwhelmingly a vote-by-mail state — so the mail-ballot ID provision would affect the vast majority of voters.
- The measure would enshrine this in the constitution, requiring the Legislature to fill in details.

Proposition 39 (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-39) would change how Californians verify their identities when voting, replacing signature matching for mail-in ballots with government-issued identification numbers and requiring identification at polling places. Hoover Institution scholar Justin Grimmer examines the proposal, the safeguards already in place, and what research reveals about voter fraud and election security. He also addresses concerns that stricter identification requirements could discourage voting, explaining why studies suggest their effects on turnout and election outcomes are minimal. Grimmer also explores whether Proposition 39 could strengthen public trust in California's elections.
ABOUT THE SERIES
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.
Launching in advance of the 2026 election, California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides) will answer the questions Californians are already asking (from housing affordability and energy costs to education, public safety, state finances, and election administration) while also explaining how California government works and what the governor, Legislature, and ballot initiatives can and cannot change. More than an election resource, California Decides is intended to become Hoover’s permanent platform for California civic education: a trusted destination where voters, policymakers, journalists, educators, and community leaders can find clear, evidence-based explanations of the state’s most important challenges and the choices that will shape its future.

California Decides (https://www.hoover.org/publications/proposition-lab-california-decides)
Summary
A sound election system has to do two things simultaneously: Prevent voter fraud while ensuring that every eligible vote is counted. Proposition 39 is arguably an attempt to improve electoral confidence while minimizing negative effects on ballot access.
Proposition 39 requires that voters provide either state-issued identification to vote in person or the last four digits of a government-issued identification number to vote by mail-in ballot, similar to many other states. It also requires that elections officials publish regular eligibility audits of voter rolls. Lastly, it mandates that California create an alternate state ID card so that those who don’t have other forms of ID, like a driver’s license, are able to vote.
Given that over 80 percent of California voters make use of mail-in ballots, Proposition 39’s greatest impacts will be on mail-in voting rather than in-person voting. California’s recent shift to all-mail elections has vastly expanded the ease of voting and, as a result, voter participation. It also has opened up a new, more rewarding avenue for voter fraud. There is no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California. Yet instances of fraud have been uncovered, and the increase of mail-in voting has coincided with decreasing confidence in the honesty of elections.
Because California’s existing election systems already requires elections officials to contact voters—by mail, email, and phone—to “cure” their mail-in ballot of any deficiencies and allows voters twenty-two days after Election Day to do so, expanding identification requirements does not seem likely to substantially inhibit valid votes from being counted.
Realistically, there is an inherent trade-off between election legitimacy and making voting easy. This measure effectively asks voters whether increased legitimacy is worth making voting slightly more difficult.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The original title was “Establishes Additional Voter Identification and Citizenship Verification Requirements” but this was changed by the California attorney general to “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification.” Ballot measure proponents challenged the new name as misleading, but the deputy attorney general argued that the title is only misleading if read in isolation. The Sacramento Superior Court ruled the changed title and summary were “sufficient.”
Measure’s own name: The California Voter ID Initiative (AG No. 25-0007A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: Voters must show government-issued ID to vote in person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number on their mail-in ballot envelopes. The state must offer a free voter ID card and conduct regular audits of voter rolls to verify eligibility and citizenship.
A vote NO means: California keeps its current system, which asks for no ID at the polls and verifies mail ballots by signature match.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0007A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0007 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-007)
1. What would it do?
More than two-thirds of states require a voter to provide identification to receive a ballot, and recent national polls by the Pew Research Center, Rasmussen Reports, and Gallup show that over 75 percent of US adults support photo ID requirements to vote. California is one of the remaining states that does not ask for any identification for in-person voting. Under this measure, anyone voting in person would have to present a government-issued ID to receive a ballot.
A similar requirement would apply to mail-in ballots. Under the measure, a mail-in voter would have to write the last four digits of a unique government-issued identification number (such as Social Security number, driver’s license number, or Voter ID card) on the ballot envelope. That number would be matched against the voter’s registration record before the ballot is counted.
For context, Minnesota already uses a similar system that requires a voter-specific identification number to verify mail-in ballots. To further ensure election integrity, Minnesota law also requires that absentee voters show their blank ballot to a witness (who must be a US citizen, notary, or public official) prior to the voter filling it out, and then requires that witness’s signature on the signature envelope certifying that the ballot was completed privately. Before the ballot is recorded at least two members of the absentee ballot board (either election officials or representatives of different political parties) review each signature envelope to ensure that it matches the voter’s name, address, signature, and voter identification number and has a witness signature.
Proposition 39 includes three more parts to facilitate voter identification and the validation of voter rolls. First, it requires the state to provide a free voter ID card on request, reducing the ballot access issues that can be caused by using a driver’s license as the default identification. Second, it requires the California Secretary of State’s office and county election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, use government data to verify citizenship attestations, and publicly report each year what share of the rolls has been citizenship-verified. Lastly, it is self-executing, such that every two years the California State Auditor’s Office must publish an audit of state and county election officials’ compliance. It also empowers any citizen to seek judicial review and remedy if they believe that state or county officials are not complying with the constitutional amendment.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0007A1, “California Voter ID Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0007A1%20((Voter%20ID)).pdf) (as amended August 7, 2025)
Key language: “Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration.”
What it amends:
Adds Section 3.1 to Article II of the California Constitution, the article that governs voting. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot simply repeal it, and it directs the legislature to enact implementing laws and to provide for military and overseas voters consistent with federal law.
3. Who, What, Where, When, Why?
What would it change about voting?
It would require a government-issued ID for in-person voting or the provision of the last four digits of a government ID number for mail voting. It requires the state to provide a free state ID card on request. Lastly, it mandates that the state regularly verify the citizenship of registered voters and report the results of that audit.
Where would it take effect?
Statewide, in every election.
When would it take effect?
The measure is self-executing on passage, such that the legislature is directed to enact implementing laws, and the state auditor is directed to publish an audit of compliance by state and county election officials in every odd-numbered year.
Why add identification rules to the voting process?
The proponents’ stated goals for this measure are to promote public confidence in the electoral process and voting results by deterring and detecting fraud, confirming voter eligibility, and minimizing voter impersonation.
4. Trade-offs
The 2020 presidential election results were controversially challenged as being manipulated by widespread voter fraud—an allegation that was believed by three out of every eight voters. The extensive mail-in voting allowed due to COVID-19 pandemic concerns was blamed as part of this alleged fraud. However, documented cases of election fraud are rare, and the most rigorous review of the 2020 election did not find evidence to support claims of systematic fraud.
A more general issue is that voter fraud statistics only measure the fraud that we have been able to detect and, more importantly, the fraud that was perpetrated within the system as it previously existed. The next sections examine:
The ways that elections have substantially changed over the last fifty years, with major changes accelerating over the last decade
How these changes provide a rational argument for those concerned with voter fraud
How the changes, at least in part, seem to be linked to declining voter confidence in elections
The type of fraud inhibited by ID requirements for in-person voting—where one person impersonates another at the polling place—is the rarest documented form of voter fraud. This doesn’t make in-person voter identification unimportant, but in-person voter fraud is arguably the smallest part of the problem. The elephant in the room, so to speak, is the significant increase in mail-in voting.
In brief summary, California’s mail-in voting system verifies eligibility mainly through the voter’s own attestation that they are who they say they are and by matching their signature to a previous signature on record (see the California Decides FAQ: How Elections Are Run (https://www.hoover.org/research/how-elections-are-run) for additional information). The lack of a rigorous means to validate who specifically filled out the mail-in ballot—which is done in private, far away from the public view of voting centers—increases the potential for voter fraud. Furthermore, the lack of clearer voter identification mechanisms means that investigations into whether voter fraud occurred will struggle to definitively certify the lack of fraud. That validation gap is precisely the proponents’ argument for building a more complete verification infrastructure.
Changes to US Elections
US elections have seen major changes since states started expanding absentee mail-in voting in the 1970s. This, like early in-person voting, has led to large decreases in voting at public polling locations on Election Day. In the last two presidential elections, over 80 percent of Californians voted by mail.
At the national level:
In-person voting on Election Day has been steadily decreasing, from around 90 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 60 percent in 2016. That percentage dropped to 31 percent in 2020 and recovered slightly to 40 percent in 2024.
Meanwhile, absentee/mail-in voting has been steadily increasing, from around 8 percent of votes cast in the mid-1990s to 21 percent of votes cast in 2016. During the pandemic mail-in ballots surged to 43 percent of votes cast in 2020 and then returned to the previous trend, accounting for 29 percent of votes in 2024.
Early in-person voting has seen a similar upward trajectory, from 2–3 percent of votes cast in the 1990s to 19 percent in 2016. The trend has accelerated faster than mail-in voting, with early in-person voting accounting for 26 percent of votes cast in 2020 and 31 percent of votes cast in 2024.
The shift away from in-person voting on Election Day seems to have increased voter anxiety about the electoral process, perhaps due to the reduced ability to identify fraud and therefore a perception that fraud would be easier to employ. Currently, eight states now practice all-mail elections (where every eligible voter receives a ballot by mail), twenty-nine more allow no-excuse absentee voting, and forty-seven allow some form of early in-person voting.
California was the first state to allow no-excuse absentee voting, starting in 1979. By 2012, a majority of California ballots were submitted by mail. Starting in 2018, the state allowed county elections officials to shift to an all-mail election, and the state itself adopted an all-mail ballot starting in 2020. This led to over 86 percent of ballots being cast by mail in 2020, followed by over 80 percent in 2024.
Concerns about Ballot Harvesting
In California, concerns about voter fraud have probably been exacerbated by legislation passed in 2016 that legalized unlimited third-party ballot collection, a practice that is more generally known as ballot harvesting. It allows any person to collect and submit any number of mail-in ballots, including paid campaign workers and volunteer advocates. The same year, other legislation enabled county election officials to mail every registered voter a ballot, expand early in-person voting, and create ballot drop box locations with 24/7 access.
In theory, the mail-in ballots should already be filled out and sealed when given to the ballot harvester, such that there’s little opportunity for the harvester to view or change the vote. There is no way to ensure this, but it’s also relevant to highlight that changing another person’s ballot (or filling it out without their approval) has never been legal and is the most fundamental form of voter fraud.
Opponents of ballot harvesting argue that the practice breaks the intrinsic chain of custody for mail-in ballots—from the voter to US Postal Service staff to elections officials—and therefore impugns the integrity of such ballots. Proponents argue that it enables greater voter participation. Both things can be simultaneously true: Many voters likely find it easier to vote, and unscrupulous political agents also have greater ability to practice fraud (regardless of whether they have actually exercised that ability to date or have done so in statistically measurable ways).
By law, the ballot harvester is required to provide their name and signature on the ballot return envelope. However, there currently doesn’t seem to be any way to validate that ballot harvesters are adhering to this requirement, because there’s nothing that distinguishes a ballot submitted by a ballot harvester from one submitted by the voter. The current system effectively places ballot harvesters on the honor system to provide that information on each ballot they submit via mail or ballot drop box, because without providing that information it appears to the elections officials that the voter submitted the ballot themselves.
Decreasing Voter Confidence and Perceived Election Honesty
At the national level, voters’ confidence in whether their own vote is counted correctly is generally high, but there is reduced confidence in whether national voting in general is counted correctly. There is also clearly declining confidence in the general honesty of elections.
It’s important to note that while voter confidence has indeed decreased over recent decades, in the short run a major part of this sentiment seems to be driven by whether a voter’s preferred candidate won the election (called the winner-loser effect). This can be particularly seen in the 2024 election, when Republican-leaning voters went into the election with very low confidence in whether their vote would be counted and then reported greater confidence in US elections following President Trump’s victory. Democratic-leaning voters shifted in the opposite direction, but the size of the change was not as substantial.
5. Conclusion
Passage of Proposition 39 would bring California into line with most other states. Voter ID requirements receive broad, bipartisan support—more than 75 percent of voters support requiring a photo ID to vote—and the ballot measure addresses a real gap in how the state verifies voter eligibility.
The trade-off for greater electoral confidence is that voter ID requirements can cause some eligible ballots to be rejected for honest mistakes. However, the legislature can effectively solve this problem by employing a system similar to that which California already uses, which requires election officials to contact voters to rectify problems with the identification the voter submitted and provides twenty-two days after Election Day to do so.
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

California currently has a statutory signature cure process (22 days), but whether that would extend to ID number mismatches depends on the Legislature acting.

Also notable: "verifying that the person has cast only one ballot in the election" — plus the requirement that the ballot is counted "only after verifying the identity" — means every VBM ballot's last-4 must match the designated ID in the registration record. Voters who registered decades ago may not remember which ID number they designated; the measure requires the type of ID to be noted on the mail ballot envelope and available by phone/electronically — that mitigates somewhat (Texas had a similar problem where voters used the wrong number — the envelope will note which type, but not the number itself).

California's vote-by-mail share (~85%) makes this the dominant effect. The claimed trust benefit is empirically unsupported by multiple studies. Fraud of the type targeted is rare even by conservative sources' own databases (Heritage: 0.02 cases/100K/year). Cost: tens of millions to low hundreds of millions/year.

# My answer: **No**

Here's how I got there, based on extensive research into the measure itself, the Legislative Analyst's analysis, the academic literature, and real-world evidence from states that have tried this.

## What Prop 39 actually does

It's a constitutional amendment that would require government ID for in-person voting, and — critically — would require the last four digits of a government ID number (matching the one on your registration) on every mail ballot envelope, or the ballot doesn't get counted. It also adds citizenship-verification "best efforts," a free state voter ID card, and audits.

## Why the evidence points to No

**1. The fraud it targets is vanishingly rare.** In-person voter impersonation — the thing voter ID prevents — is the rarest documented form of fraud. Even the Heritage Foundation's own database (the strongest pro-ID source) documents only about 0.02–0.08 cases per 100,000 people per year, and most rigorous studies find no detectable effect of ID laws on fraud. Even the Hoover Institution's sympathetic analysis concedes there's "no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California."

**2. The mail-ballot provision has a documented track record of failure — in a state that votes overwhelmingly by mail.** ~85% of California ballots are cast by mail, so this provision is the measure's real core. Texas passed a nearly identical rule (ID number must match your registration record on the envelope). The result in the first election: mail ballot rejections jumped from ~1% to **12.4%**, roughly 30,000 voters had applications or ballots rejected, ~90% never ended up participating, and Black, Latino, and Asian voters were rejected at significantly higher rates than white voters. That's orders of magnitude more eligible voters disenfranchised than fraudulent votes prevented.

**3. The core rationale — "increasing trust in elections" — is empirically unsupported.** This is the striking part: multiple peer-reviewed studies (Cantoni & Pons, Ansolabehere & Persily, Stewart et al., Bowler et al.) consistently find that voter ID laws do **not** increase voter confidence or reduce perceived fraud. If anything, the polarized fight over them seems to reduce trust. So the main claimed benefit doesn't materialize, while the rejection costs do.

**4. Real costs and implementation risk.** The Legislative Analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year — and notes savings would partly come from *fewer registered voters, including eligible voters lacking ID*. Notably, the amendment itself contains **no cure process** for mismatched or missing ID digits (unlike California's current 22-day signature cure window); it leaves those details to implementing legislation in a Legislature whose leadership opposes the measure — a recipe for a botched rollout.

## The strongest Yes arguments (which I took seriously)

- Standard polling-place ID laws have shown little to no measurable turnout decline in the best recent research (Cantoni & Pons), so the "suppression" charge is weaker than opponents claim.
- Voter ID polls at 75%+ nationally including majorities of Democrats; most states require some ID.
- The free voter ID card addresses access concerns, and ID numbers are arguably more reliable than signature matching (though California's signature system rejects only ~0.9% of mail ballots, with a cure process — vs. Texas's 12% under ID matching).

## Bottom line

The trade the measure offers is: spend tens-to-hundreds of millions annually and risk Texas-style ballot rejection rates for 13+ million mail voters, in exchange for deterring a nearly nonexistent form of fraud and a trust boost that research shows doesn't actually materialize. The costs are demonstrated and large; the benefits are hypothetical and empirically unproven. **Vote No.**
